title: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
summary: Why models break past their trained length, how PI, NTK, YaRN, base scaling and LongRoPE fix RoPE, how Ring Attention and context parallelism fit million-token attention, and how to test it.
outcomes: Explain why RoPE pairs whose wavelength exceeds the trained length break when the context is extended
Compute PI, NTK-aware and YaRN frequency scales and the YaRN attention factor for a given model and scale factor
Explain how base-frequency changes (ABF), searched factors (LongRoPE) and long-data training extend context
Explain how Ring Attention computes exact attention, forward and backward, by rotating KV blocks with an online softmax
Compute prefill FLOPs and the minimum block size c >= (H_kv / H) F / B, and balance causal work across ranks
Choose pass-KV or pass-Q context parallelism for long-context prefill and decode
Evaluate long-context models with passkey, Lost in the Middle and RULER instead of perplexity alone

lessons.title: Why models break past their trained length

blocks.md:
A transformer is trained on sequences up to some length $L$, its **context window** (2,048 tokens for Meta's LLaMA, 4,096 for Llama 2, 8,192 for Llama 3). Feed it a longer prompt and quality usually collapses, even though nothing in the weights depends on sequence length. Two separate walls stand in the way:

1. **The position encoding wall.** The model has never seen the position signals that appear past $L$, so attention scores become out of distribution. Out of distribution means unlike any input seen in training: the weights were fitted only to those inputs, so their output on new ones is unpredictable.
2. **The memory and compute wall.** Attention compares every token with every other, so cost grows with the square of the length, and even the KV cache outgrows one GPU.

This course takes them in order: lessons 2 to 4 fix the first wall by changing RoPE (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN, base scaling, searched factors), lessons 5 and 6 break the second (Ring Attention, context parallelism), lesson 7 builds both in NumPy, and lesson 8 asks whether the model actually *uses* the longer context.

Recall from the attention course that a score is the dot product $q_m^\top k_n$ of a query at position $m$ and a key at position $n$. **RoPE** (rotary position embedding, Su et al., from the paper that introduced the RoFormer model) injects position by *rotating* those vectors instead of adding a position vector to the input. The head dimension $|D|$ is the length of each query and key vector in one attention head, the attention course's $d_k$ (the YaRN paper writes it $|D|$). It is split into $|D|/2$ pairs of numbers, and each pair is treated as a point in a plane. Rotating a point $(x, y)$ by an angle $\phi$ gives $(x\cos\phi - y\sin\phi,\ x\sin\phi + y\cos\phi)$, so implementations precompute tables of $\cos$ and $\sin$ for every position and pair. Pair $d$ of the token at position $m$ is rotated by the angle $m\theta_d$, where $\theta_d$ is the pair's frequency in radians per token:

blocks.caption: theta_d is b to the power minus 2d over |D|, so each pair turns slower than the one before by the same factor. The base b is 10000 in RoFormer and Llama 2 (Llama 3 raises it to 500,000). The wavelength lambda_d is how many tokens pair d needs for one full turn (notation from the YaRN paper).

blocks.md:
Why relative? Within one pair, a dot product depends only on the two vectors' lengths and the angle between them. Rotating $q$ by $m\theta$ and $k$ by $n\theta$ changes that angle by $(m-n)\theta$, so the score depends only on the *relative* distance $m-n$, not on where the two tokens sit. Low $d$ pairs spin fast (short wavelength) and resolve nearby order; high $d$ pairs spin slowly and act like a coarse clock over the whole window.

The wavelength follows from one full turn being $2\pi$ radians: at $\theta_d$ radians per token, pair $d$ is back at its start after $\lambda_d = 2\pi/\theta_d$ tokens.

Take a toy head with $|D| = 8$ (4 pairs), $b = 10000$, trained on $L = 2048$. Then $\theta_d = 10000^{-2d/8} = 10^{-d}$, so $\theta = 1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001$ radians per token, and dividing $2\pi$ by each gives wavelengths of 6.3, 62.8, 628.3 and 6,283.2 tokens.

blocks.title: Toy RoPE: which angles did training ever show?

scenes.caption: Wavelength and r = L / lambda, the number of full turns each pair makes across the 2,048 training positions. Pairs 0 to 2 wrap around many times; pair 3 completes only a third of a turn.
Angle (radians) at position 2047, the last trained position. Pair 3 has only ever seen angles between 0 and 2.047 rad.

At position 4095 pair 3 sits at 4.095 rad, an angle it never saw. Pairs 0 to 2 wrapped during training, so every angle on their circle is familiar. The fast pairs are fine; the slow pair is out of distribution.

blocks.md: Columns: wavelength $\lambda$, rotations $r = L/\lambda$, angle at position 2047, angle at position 4095. The same split happens in real models. For Llama 2 ($|D| = 128$, $b = 10000$, $L = 4096$), pairs 0 to 45 complete at least one turn within 4,096 tokens, but the 18 pairs $d = 46$ to $63$ have $\lambda > 4096$ (pair 63: about 54,410 tokens). Where does 46 come from? Here $\lambda_d = 2\pi \cdot 10000^{2d/128} = 2\pi \cdot 10^{d/16}$. Setting it equal to 4096 gives $10^{d/16} \approx 652$, so $d \approx 45.03$: pair 45 just finishes a turn and pair 46 does not, and pair 63 gets $2\pi \cdot 10^{63/16} \approx 54{,}410$. Those slow pairs effectively encode *absolute* position: an angle below one turn names a single spot in the window, the way an hour hand names the time of day. Past $L$ they produce angles the network has never seen.

blocks.title: RoPE wavelength per pair versus the trained length

scenes.caption: Llama 2 setting: base 10000, L = 4096. Every pair whose wavelength curve lies above the flat line never finishes a turn during training (pairs 46 to 63).
Llama 3 setting: base 500,000, L = 8192. A larger base stretches all wavelengths, so more pairs are slow; the crossing moves to a lower pair index.

blocks.prompt: LLaMA was pretrained at 2,048 tokens. If you simply fine-tune it (keep training its pretrained weights) on 8,192-token sequences without touching RoPE, how fast do you expect the usable context to grow?
blocks.reveal: Very slowly. The Position Interpolation paper fine-tuned LLaMA directly on longer sequences and after more than 10,000 batches the effective context window only moved from 2,048 to 2,560 tokens. The slow pairs must learn brand new angles, and the attention scores they produce can be wildly large out of distribution. That is why every method in the next three lessons changes the rotation itself instead.

blocks.md: RoPE is called a relative encoding, so it is tempting to think it should extrapolate for free. It does not: dimensions whose wavelength exceeds the training length never wrap, so in practice they leak absolute position, and new positions mean new, unseen angles.

Each RoPE pair has a wavelength $\lambda_d = 2\pi b^{2d/|D|}$. Pairs with $\lambda_d \ll L$ are safe at any length; pairs with $\lambda_d > L$ are the ones that break when you go past the trained window.

blocks.question: In the toy head (wavelengths 6.3, 62.8, 628.3, 6,283 tokens; trained on 2,048), which pair sees an out-of-distribution angle first as the prompt grows past 2,048 tokens?
options: Pair 0, because it rotates fastest and accumulates the largest angle
Pair 3, because it never completed a full turn during training
All pairs equally, because every position past 2,048 is new
None, because RoPE only depends on relative distance
blocks.explain: Pair 0 reaches huge raw angles but wraps every 6.3 tokens, so every angle on its circle was seen thousands of times. Pair 3 only ever covered 0 to 2.047 rad, so at position 2,100 it is already at 2.1 rad, outside its training range.

blocks.question: Raising the RoPE base b (as Llama 3 does with 500,000) changes the wavelengths how?
options: Every wavelength except pair 0's gets longer, so more pairs act as slow, absolute-position pairs
All wavelengths get shorter, so every pair wraps within the window
Only pair 0 changes
Wavelengths are fixed by the head dimension, not by b
blocks.explain: lambda_d = 2 pi b^(2d/|D|) grows with b for every d above 0 (pair 0 always has wavelength 2 pi). A bigger base spreads frequencies over a longer range, which is why it is used together with long-context training.

blocks.md: **Position Interpolation (PI)**, from Chen et al. at Meta (2023), makes one change: instead of feeding position $m$, feed $m/s$, where $s = L'/L$ is the **scale factor** from the trained length $L$ to the target $L'$. Every position in the long sequence is squeezed back into the trained range $[0, L)$, so no pair ever sees a new angle. Positions become fractional, which RoPE handles fine because angles are continuous.

blocks.caption: f(x, m) is RoPE: it rotates the vector x as if it sat at position m. PI calls it with m over s instead of m. Equivalently every frequency theta_d is divided by s.

blocks.md:
Why is that safer? Treat one head's attention score as a function $a(\Delta)$ of the relative distance $\Delta$. Training pins it down at integer distances; PI only asks for values *between* two neighbouring ones. The paper proves that between them the score can stray from the straight line joining its two trained values by at most $|D| \max_j |h_j| / (32 \ln b)$, where $h_j$ is the query-key product of pair $j$. The RoFormer bound for a score at an arbitrary *new* distance (extrapolation) is at least about 600 times larger in the LLaMA 7B setting. The paper also extends LLaMA 7B to 65B to 32,768 tokens with at most 1,000 fine-tuning steps.

The cost is precision. Interpolation shrinks *every* pair by $s$, including the fast ones that tell neighbouring tokens apart. In the toy head with $s = 4$, pair 0 now turns 0.25 rad per token instead of 1 rad, so adjacent tokens look four times closer than anything the model was trained on. The YaRN paper reports PI fine-tunes only reached roughly $s = 8$ before outputs degraded.

blocks.title: How much each method slows each RoPE pair (toy head, s = 4)

scenes.caption: Original RoPE: every pair keeps its trained frequency (factor 1). At position 4095 pair 3 hits 4.095 rad, outside the 0 to 2.047 rad it saw in training.
PI divides every frequency by s = 4. Pair 3 at position 4095 is now at 1.024 rad (seen), but pair 0 also slows to 0.25 rad per token: nearby tokens get blurred.

NTK-aware (explained next) raises the base to b' = 10000 x 4^(8/6), about 63,496. The fastest pair keeps factor 1, the slowest gets exactly 1 over s, and the middle pairs fall in between (0.63, 0.397).

blocks.md: **NTK-aware interpolation** (posted on Reddit by the user bloc97 in 2023, written up in the YaRN paper, Appendix A.2) spreads the "interpolation pressure" unevenly: scale high frequencies less and low frequencies more. NTK stands for neural tangent kernel, a theory of how wide networks learn. Using it, Tancik et al. (2020) showed that networks struggle to learn high-frequency detail from a low-dimensional input unless its embedding keeps high-frequency components. A position is a one-dimensional input and RoPE's fast pairs are its high-frequency components, so NTK-aware scaling leaves them almost untouched.

The simplest way is to change the base so that the *last* pair is slowed by exactly $s$ while pair 0 is untouched. The last pair, $d = |D|/2 - 1$, has $\theta = b^{-(|D|-2)/|D|}$. We want a new base $b'$ with $b'^{-(|D|-2)/|D|} = b^{-(|D|-2)/|D|}/s$. Raising both sides to the power $-|D|/(|D|-2)$ gives the new base, and putting it back into $\theta_d = b'^{-2d/|D|}$ gives each pair's slowdown:

blocks.caption: In words: the new base is b times s to the power |D| over (|D| minus 2), and pair d's frequency is multiplied by s to the power minus 2d over (|D| minus 2), which is 1 for pair 0 and exactly 1 over s for the last pair.

blocks.md: For Llama 2 ($|D| = 128$) and $s = 16$, $b' \approx 167{,}199$. The per-pair slowdown then rises smoothly from 1.0 at pair 0 to 2.0 at pair 16, 4.1 at pair 32, 8.3 at pair 48 and 16 at pair 63. Code Llama, Meta's Llama 2 model specialized for code, applied the same base-change idea, raising the base from 10,000 to 1,000,000 for long-context fine-tuning. The name adjusted base frequency (ABF) comes from Xiong et al., Effective Long-Context Scaling of Foundation Models; lesson 4 shows how ABF plus long-data training became the standard recipe.

blocks.title: Per-pair frequency multiplier: PI vs NTK-aware (Llama 2)

scenes.caption: PI multiplies every pair by 1 over s. NTK-aware keeps the fast pairs near 1 and only reaches 1 over s at the slowest pair.
At s = 16 the gap is huge: PI slows even pair 0 sixteenfold, NTK-aware leaves pairs 0 to 10 within a factor 1.6 of the original.

Notice where NTK-aware still exceeds 1 over s: pairs 46 to 62 have wavelengths above L, yet they are slowed by less than s, so at the target length they rotate past angles never seen in training (a mild extrapolation).

blocks.md: NTK-aware works much better than PI *without* fine-tuning, but the YaRN authors list two problems. Some pairs are slightly extrapolated to out-of-bound angles, so fine-tuning with it gave worse results than PI, and the nominal $s$ does not match the real extension, so in practice $s$ must be set higher than the target and the best base has to be found empirically.

Do not confuse the two knobs. PI rescales *positions* (every pair by the same $1/s$). NTK-aware changes the *base* (each pair by a different amount). Both leave the model architecture unchanged; only the precomputed cos and sin tables differ.
Uniform interpolation protects the slow pairs but blurs the fast ones. Every better method since PI is about treating pairs differently according to their wavelength.

blocks.question: A Llama 2 model (L = 4096) is extended with PI to 16,384 tokens. What position value does RoPE receive for the token at index 10,000?
options: 4,096, clipped to the trained maximum
blocks.explain: s = 16384 / 4096 = 4, and PI feeds m / s = 10000 / 4 = 2500. Positions are scaled, not clipped; fractional values are allowed.

blocks.question: Why does PI hurt the fast (low d) RoPE pairs?
options: They overflow numerically at large positions
They are dropped entirely
Their wavelength becomes longer than the context, so they stop encoding anything
Dividing their frequency by s makes neighbouring tokens differ by a much smaller angle than in training, so local order is harder to resolve
blocks.explain: Pair 0 normally turns 1 rad per token; after PI with s = 4 it turns 0.25 rad. Nearby tokens become nearly indistinguishable in that pair, the high-frequency information the network relied on.

lessons.title: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature

blocks.md:
YaRN (Yet another RoPE extensioN method; Peng, Quesnelle, Fan, Shippole, 2023) makes the per-pair treatment explicit. It measures each pair by $r(d) = L/\lambda_d$, the number of full turns the pair makes during training, and applies a three-way rule that the paper calls **NTK-by-parts** (it builds on NTK-aware scaling but treats the pairs in separate parts), with two thresholds on the turn count, $\alpha < \beta$:

- $r(d) > \beta$: many turns, the pair only encodes relative position. **Do not touch it.**
- $r(d) < \alpha$: less than one turn, the pair encodes absolute position. **Interpolate it fully, like PI** (never extrapolate).
- in between: blend linearly.

For the LLaMA family the paper found $\alpha = 1$ and $\beta = 32$ work well. The paper writes every method as a change of the position $m$ into $g(m)$ and of each frequency $\theta_d$ into $h(\theta_d)$. YaRN leaves positions as they are ($g(m) = m$); only the frequencies change.

blocks.caption: YaRN Eq. 11 and 13. The ramp gamma is 0 below alpha, 1 above beta, and (r minus alpha) over (beta minus alpha) between. The new frequency mixes (1 minus gamma) times theta_d over s with gamma times theta_d, so gamma = 1 keeps it and gamma = 0 divides it by s.

blocks.title: YaRN on the toy head (L = 2048, s = 4)
blocks.code:
import math
b, D, L, s = 10000, 8, 2048, 4   # toy: 4 rotary pairs
alpha, beta = 1, 32              # ramp bounds (paper's Llama values)
for d in range(D // 2):
    theta = b ** (-2 * d / D)
    lam = 2 * math.pi / theta    # wavelength in tokens
    r = L / lam                  # rotations seen in training
    g = min(max((r - alpha) / (beta - alpha), 0), 1)
    scale = (1 - g) / s + g      # 1 = keep, 1/s = interpolate
    print(d, round(lam, 1), round(r, 2), round(g, 3), round(scale, 4))
mscale = 0.1 * math.log(s) + 1   # multiplies cos and sin
print("mscale", round(mscale, 4), "logits x", round(mscale ** 2, 4))

scenes.caption: Setup: 4 rotary pairs, trained length 2048, target 8192 (s = 4), ramp bounds alpha = 1 and beta = 32.
Pair 0: wavelength 6.3 tokens, 325.95 turns during training. r is above beta, so gamma = 1 and the frequency is kept.
Pair 1: 32.59 turns, just above beta = 32, so it is also kept intact.
Pair 2: 3.26 turns sits inside the ramp. gamma = (3.26 - 1) / 31 = 0.073, so the scale is 0.927 / 4 + 0.073 = 0.3047, mostly interpolated.
Pair 3: a third of a turn, r is below alpha, so gamma = 0 and it is fully interpolated (1 over s = 0.25), exactly like PI.
Finally the attention temperature (explained below): cos and sin are multiplied by 0.1 ln 4 + 1 = 1.1386, which multiplies every logit by 1.2965.

blocks.md: At real scale, Llama 2 extended with $s = 16$ ($L = 4096$): pairs 0 to 20 have $r > 32$ and are untouched, pairs 46 to 63 have $r < 1$ and are divided by 16, and pairs 21 to 45 blend (pair 32, for example, has $r = 6.52$, $\gamma = 0.178$, and keeps 0.229 of its frequency). Hugging Face (HF), whose transformers library loads most open models, computes the same boundaries in closed form: solving $L/\lambda_d = \beta$ and $L/\lambda_d = \alpha$ for $d$ gives fractional pair indices 20.94 and 45.03, which it floors and ceils to 20 and 46. Between them HF ramps linearly in pair index, not in $r$, so middle pairs differ from the paper's rule (pair 32 keeps about 0.567 of its frequency in HF, not 0.229).

blocks.title: YaRN ramp: frequency multiplier per pair (Llama 2, head dim 128)

scenes.caption: s = 16, alpha = 1, beta = 32: a flat 1 for the fast pairs, a flat 1/16 for the slow pairs, and a ramp between them. Compare the PI line at 1/s.
Add NTK-aware: it slows fast pairs a little (pair 16 by 2x) and under-slows pairs near the boundary. YaRN instead never touches pairs with more than 32 turns and never extrapolates the slow ones.
Narrow the ramp (beta = 8): more pairs keep their frequency. The boundaries are tuned per model family; the paper's Llama values are 1 and 32.

blocks.md: The second ingredient is a **temperature** $t$ on the attention logits. Logits are the raw scores that go into the softmax, here $q_m^\top k_n/\sqrt{|D|}$. Dividing every logit by $t$ before the softmax is called temperature after the same knob in physics' Boltzmann distribution, which has this form: $t > 1$ flattens the weights toward uniform, $t < 1$ sharpens them toward the top score. The authors observed that dividing logits by a suitable $t$ lowers perplexity uniformly across samples and positions of the extended window. Perplexity, from the attention course, is $e$ raised to the average negative log-probability of each correct next token: the number of equally likely choices the model is as unsure as, so lower is better. There is no derivation behind the best $t$: the authors fitted it on LLaMA 7B to 65B:

blocks.caption: YaRN Eq. 14 and 15. Each logit is divided by t on top of the usual square root of |D|, and the square root of 1 over t is 0.1 times ln s plus 1. For s = 8 this gives 1.208; for s = 16, 1.2773, so logits are multiplied by 1 over t = 1.6314.

blocks.md: No attention code changes: since both $q$ and $k$ are rotated by the RoPE tables, multiplying cos and sin by $\sqrt{1/t}$ scales the logit by $1/t$. In Hugging Face transformers this is the `attention_factor` that the YaRN rope function returns alongside the new frequencies (default `0.1 * log(factor) + 1`, where factor is $s$ and log is the natural log). The factor is above 1, so it *sharpens* attention, offsetting the flatter distribution you get when a query is spread over many more keys.

blocks.title: YaRN attention factor versus scale factor

scenes.caption: The multiplier on cos and sin grows slowly with s: 1.069 at s = 2, 1.208 at s = 8, 1.347 at s = 32.
The logit multiplier is its square: 1.143, 1.459 and 1.813 at the same scales. The effect is real but gentle, logarithmic in s.

blocks.md: The next figure compares the methods on Proof-pile, a public dataset of mathematical text and code (arXiv papers, books, formal math libraries, Stack Exchange) whose long documents suit long-context tests.

blocks.title: LLaMA 7B Proof-pile perplexity (YaRN Table 5, lower is better)

scenes.caption: No fine-tuning, s = 2, evaluated at 4,096 tokens. NTK-aware is worst here (5.97); YaRN 3.67 is best, just ahead of NTK-by-parts (3.71).
Fine-tuned 400 steps with s = 16, evaluated at 32,768 tokens: NTK-aware degrades to 8.49 while YaRN reaches 2.77, slightly ahead of NTK-by-parts (2.81) thanks to the temperature.

blocks.md: The paper fine-tuned Llama 2 7B and 13B with $s = 16$ for 400 steps (batch 64, 64K-token chunks of PG19, a dataset of Project Gutenberg books published before 1919), then $s = 32$ for 200 more, reaching 128K. It reports needing about 10x fewer tokens and 2.5x fewer training steps than previous methods. **Dynamic scaling** is an inference-only variant: recompute $s = \max(1, l'/L)$ from the current length $l'$ on every forward pass, so short prompts run unscaled.

With dynamic scaling the RoPE of every cached token changes when $s$ changes. The YaRN paper notes the correct implementation caches keys *before* applying RoPE; caching rotated keys silently mixes two different scalings.

Here is the problem with numbers. Take Llama 2's pair 50: wavelength 8,379 tokens, so $r = 0.49$ and YaRN divides its frequency by the full $s$. With dynamic scaling at 3,000 tokens, $s = 1$, and the keys at positions 1,000, 2,000 and 3,000 are cached already rotated by $n\theta$. The prompt then grows to 5,120 tokens, so $s = 5120/4096 = 1.25$, and new tokens are rotated by $n\theta/1.25$. For simplicity the figure uses unit vectors in this one pair, so a score is just the cosine of the angle between query and key.

blocks.title: Dynamic scaling with a rotated-key cache (Llama 2 pair 50)

scenes.caption: At 3,000 tokens s = 1. Keys are cached rotated by n theta (theta = 0.00075 rad per token). The query at 3,000 sits at 2.250 rad; scores are cosines of the angle gaps.

The prompt reaches 5,120 tokens, so s = 1.25. The query at 5,119 is rotated by 5119 theta / 1.25 = 3.071 rad and the new key at 5,000 by 3.000, but the cached keys keep their old angles. Mixed scalings: 0.681 for the key at 3,000.
Correct: cache keys before RoPE and rotate all of them with s = 1.25 (0.600, 1.200, 1.800). The key at 3,000 now scores 0.295, not 0.681. The rotated cache silently changed the attention pattern.

blocks.md: **Llama 3.1** ships its own by-parts rule. Meta's reference `apply_scaling` uses factor 8 (that is $s$), low_freq_factor 1, high_freq_factor 4 and an original length of 8,192 with base 500,000 (comment: "Values obtained from grid search"). The two factors set wavelength thresholds: pairs with wavelength under 8192 over high_freq_factor 4 = 2,048 tokens are kept, those over 8192 over low_freq_factor 1 = 8,192 are divided by 8, and those between are smoothed. With head dim 128 that is 29 kept pairs, 6 smoothed and 29 divided. Unlike YaRN there is no attention factor (Hugging Face returns 1.0 for `rope_type: llama3`).

blocks.code:
# Hugging Face config fields (rope_scaling, called rope_parameters in newer versions)
# Llama 3.1 style: by-parts on wavelength thresholds, no temperature
{"rope_type": "llama3", "rope_theta": 500000.0, "factor": 8.0,
 "low_freq_factor": 1.0, "high_freq_factor": 4.0,
 "original_max_position_embeddings": 8192}

# YaRN: required keys; beta_fast / beta_slow default to 32 / 1
{"rope_type": "yarn", "factor": 4.0,
 "original_max_position_embeddings": 32768}
blocks.caption: Key names follow the validators in transformers' modeling_rope_utils.py. The YaRN example values are illustrative, not from a specific model card.

blocks.md: YaRN = per-pair ramp on rotations $r = L/\lambda$ (keep fast pairs, fully interpolate slow ones, blend between) plus a logit temperature $\sqrt{1/t} = 0.1\ln s + 1$, all baked into the precomputed cos and sin tables.

blocks.question: Under YaRN with alpha = 1 and beta = 32, a RoPE pair completes 50 full turns within the original training length. What happens to its frequency when you extend by s = 8?
options: It is unchanged
It is divided by 8
It is divided by about 4, halfway along the ramp
It is multiplied by 8 to compensate
blocks.explain: r = 50 is above beta = 32, so gamma = 1 and h(theta) = theta. High-frequency pairs only carry relative position, which is already in distribution at any length.

blocks.question: A colleague implements YaRN by scaling queries by 1.2773 for s = 16 but forgets the keys. What is the effect on the logits?
options: Correct: the temperature is defined on queries only
Logits are unchanged because softmax is scale invariant
Logits are scaled by 1.2773 instead of the intended 1.6314
Logits are scaled by 1.6314 squared
blocks.explain: YaRN multiplies both rotated q and k (via cos and sin) by sqrt(1/t) = 0.1 ln 16 + 1 = 1.2773, so the dot product is scaled by 1.2773 squared = 1.6314. Scaling only one side gives just 1.2773. Softmax is shift invariant, not scale invariant.

blocks.question: For Llama 3.1 (base 500,000, original length 8,192, factor 8, high_freq_factor 4), a pair has wavelength 1,500 tokens. How is it scaled?
options: Divided by 8
Smoothed between 1 and 1/8
Kept unchanged
Divided by 4
blocks.explain: High-frequency threshold = 8192 / 4 = 2048 tokens. A wavelength of 1,500 is below it, so the frequency is kept. Only wavelengths above 8,192 are divided by 8, with smoothing in between.

lessons.title: Other routes to long context: base scaling, searched factors, data

blocks.md: PI, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN are recipes you can apply to a finished model with little or no training. Most recent model reports turn a different knob: they change the RoPE base $b$ and then keep training on long documents. Tiny example: the toy head from lesson 1 ($|D| = 8$) with base 10,000 has wavelengths 6.3, 62.8, 628.3 and 6,283 tokens. Raise the base to 500,000 and they become 6.3, 167.1, 4,443 and 118,143 tokens. Pair 0 is untouched, and every other pair turns more slowly, the slowest one about 19 times more slowly.

blocks.caption: Changing the base from b to b' multiplies pair d's frequency by (b over b') to the power 2d over |D|. For Llama 2's head (|D| = 128) the slowdown is 1 at pair 0, 7.07 at pair 32 and 47.0 at pair 63.

blocks.md: This is exactly the NTK-aware base change from lesson 2, taken much further: solving $b' = b\,s^{|D|/(|D|-2)}$ for $b' = 500{,}000$ with Llama 2's $|D| = 128$ gives $s \approx 47$. **Adjusted base frequency (ABF)**, from Xiong et al. (2023) at Meta, raised Llama 2's base from 10,000 to 500,000 and then continued pretraining (kept training all weights with the ordinary next-token objective) on 400B tokens over 100,000 steps, with 32,768-token sequences for 7B and 13B and 16,384 for 34B and 70B. The authors' reason is RoPE's decay: the expected query-key score shrinks as distance grows, and a larger base weakens that decay for distant tokens. ABF gave slightly lower long-sequence perplexity than PI and was the only variant that kept its score up to the full 32,768 tokens on a first-sentence retrieval task.

blocks.title: RoPE pairs that never finish a turn within the training length

scenes.caption: Head dim 128 (64 pairs), counting pairs with wavelength above the training length. Llama 2 as trained: 18 slow pairs (lesson 1). Training the same base at 32K would leave only 4.
ABF (base 500K, trained at 32K): 22 pairs stay below one turn over the whole window, and the long-data training teaches the network those slow angles directly instead of rescaling at inference time.
Llama 3 used base 500,000 from the start of pretraining at 8K (29 slow pairs), citing Xiong et al., then extended to 128K in long-context stages. Code Llama raised its base to 1,000,000.

blocks.md: Long data alone was not enough. Xiong et al. report that with Llama 2's original base the model still could not attend effectively beyond about 4,000 to 6,000 tokens after extensive long-context continual pretraining. Changing the base of a finished model without training, on the other hand, is just NTK-aware scaling with a huge s. The knob and the training go together.

Continual pretraining is also cheaper than training long from scratch: in the same paper, a 7B model that started at 4,096 tokens and switched to 32,768 partway through came close to one trained at 32,768 throughout, with about 40% fewer FLOPs.

**LongRoPE** (Ding et al., 2024, Microsoft) asks whether a closed-form rule like YaRN's ramp is leaving quality on the table. It searches instead. Each pair $i$ gets its own rescale factor, written $\lambda_i$ in the paper (not the wavelength $\lambda_d$ from lesson 1): the pair's frequency is divided by it, and the first $\hat n$ positions are left uninterpolated, because the first tokens of a sequence receive a lot of attention. An evolutionary search proposes candidate factor sets, scores each by perplexity on a few long samples and keeps mutating the best. The initial population is seeded with PI, NTK and YaRN, and candidates must be non-decreasing in $i$ (slower pairs get at least as much interpolation).

The search alone extends LLaMA 2 from 4K to 32K (8x) without fine-tuning. For more, LongRoPE goes progressively: search factors for 128K and 256K, fine-tune LLaMA 2 7B for 400 steps at 128K, swap in the 256K factors and fine-tune 600 more steps, then run a second search on the fine-tuned model to reach 2048K (512x) with no further fine-tuning. Stretching that far crowds the original 4K positions and hurts short prompts, so a final search finds separate factors for short lengths (4K and 8K), and inference switches between the sets by length.

blocks.title: Divide each pair's frequency by: Phi-3-mini-128k (head dim 96, s = 32)

scenes.caption: YaRN's closed form for this shape (base 10,000, original 4,096, s = 32, alpha 1, beta 32), computed by script: pairs 0 to 15 kept, a ramp, then a flat divide by 32 from pair 34.

The long_factor list shipped in Phi-3-mini-128k's config, which the Phi-3 report says was built with LongRoPE. It slows even fast pairs (pair 8 by 3.01) and divides the slowest by up to 64.76, twice s.
Its short_factor list, used when the sequence fits in 4,096 tokens: gentle factors from 1.1 to 3.05, the short-context readjustment.

blocks.md:
In Hugging Face transformers these lists are `long_factor` and `short_factor` under `rope_type: longrope`. The library uses the long list once the sequence is longer than `original_max_position_embeddings` and the short list otherwise, and divides each base frequency by its factor. Its default attention factor is $\sqrt{1 + \ln s / \ln L}$, which is 1.1902 for Phi-3-mini-128k ($s = 32$, $L = 4096$), a different formula from YaRN's $0.1 \ln s + 1$. Switching lists mid-generation raises the same cached-key question as dynamic scaling in lesson 3.

**ALiBi** (Press, Smith and Lewis), covered in the *Attention and the Transformer* course's lesson on relative positions, avoids the whole question: it has no rotation, only a fixed per-head penalty proportional to distance, so no new position produces an unseen rotation, and the paper shows it extrapolates well past its training length. The models in this course all use RoPE. Llama 4 (2025) mixes ideas: its iRoPE design interleaves layers with no position embedding among RoPE layers and scales attention temperature at inference.

**The data side.** Fu et al. (2024), *Data Engineering for Scaling Language Models to 128K Context*, argue that the ability to use information anywhere in a long input is mostly already learned in pretraining, so a light continual pretraining unlocks it. With Llama 2 7B and 13B, the base adjusted as in Xiong et al., 80K-token training sequences (64K for 13B) and 4M-token batches, **500 million to 5 billion tokens** were enough to retrieve a needle anywhere within 128K. The mixture matters: keep each source's share of the original pretraining mix and upsample long documents *within* each source. Upsampling only long-document domains such as books gave worse results. Training on 80K was only about 3x slower than on 4K.

The common production recipe: pick a large RoPE base (or raise it), then continue pretraining on a balanced mix with long documents upsampled, extending length in stages. Llama 3's six stages and 800B tokens (lesson 8) are the large-scale version. Inference-time rescaling (YaRN, Llama 3.1's rule, LongRoPE factors) is layered on top to go further.

blocks.prompt: Phi-3-mini-128k receives a 2,000-token prompt in Hugging Face transformers. Which factor list does it use, and what is pair 47's frequency compared with the base rule?
blocks.reveal: The short list, because 2,000 is not longer than `original_max_position_embeddings` = 4,096. Pair 47's short factor is 3.05, so its frequency is the base value divided by 3.05. Past 4,096 tokens the library switches to `long_factor`, where pair 47 is divided by 64.76.

blocks.question: A team can afford a few billion tokens of continued pretraining but no architectural change. Which knob do most recent long-context model reports turn?
options: Replace RoPE with ALiBi and retrain from scratch
Apply PI at inference only and skip training entirely
Raise the RoPE base frequency and continue pretraining on a length-upsampled, domain-balanced mix
Add more attention heads so each head covers a shorter span
blocks.explain: ABF (Xiong et al.), Code Llama and Llama 3 all change the base, and Fu et al. show 0.5B to 5B tokens of balanced, length-upsampled data suffice for 128K retrieval. Switching to ALiBi is an architecture change, and PI fine-tunes degraded past about s = 8 even with training, so skipping training entirely is worse.

blocks.question: How does LongRoPE's searched per-pair factor list differ from YaRN's ramp in Phi-3-mini-128k's released config?
options: It never rescales any pair whose wavelength is below the original length
It rescales pairs YaRN would keep (pair 8 divided by 3.01) and divides the slowest pairs by about 64, twice s = 32
It uses one factor for all pairs, like PI
It changes the base but not individual pairs
blocks.explain: The long_factor list starts at 1.07 for pair 0, reaches 3.01 at pair 8 and 64.76 at pair 47. YaRN keeps pairs 0 to 15 unchanged and caps the divisor at s = 32. The search found a non-uniform curve no closed form prescribes, then fine-tuning adapted the model to it.

blocks.md: Fixing RoPE lets the model *understand* position 100,000. It does not make position 100,000 *fit*. Take Llama 3 8B: 32 layers, 8 KV heads (grouped-query attention) of dimension 128, stored in bf16 (bfloat16, the brain floating-point format from Google Brain: 16 bits with FP32's 8 exponent bits but only 7 mantissa bits, so 2 bytes per number with FP32's range). The KV cache costs

blocks.caption: So 1 GiB at 8K tokens, 16 GiB at 128K and 128 GiB at 1M tokens, before weights or activations.

blocks.md: A naive attention that materializes the score matrix is far worse: one head at 128K tokens needs $131072^2 \times 2$ bytes = 32 GiB in bf16, *per head, per layer*. Memory-efficient (blockwise) attention, the idea behind the FlashAttention kernels (Dao et al., 2022), never stores that matrix; it streams key and value blocks and keeps a running softmax. But even then, the Ring Attention paper points out that each layer's *output* for the whole sequence must still be stored on one device, and accelerators then had less than 100 GB of HBM. Larger parts since (141 GB on NVIDIA's H200, 288 GB on AMD's MI355X) still cannot hold million-token activations for every layer.

blocks.title: Memory at long context (Llama 3 8B shapes, bf16)

scenes.caption: The KV cache grows linearly: 16 GiB at 128K tokens with 8 KV heads. Slide KV heads to 32 to see why grouped-query attention matters (64 GiB).
A materialized score matrix grows quadratically: 32 GiB for a single head at 128K and 2 TiB at 1M. This is the term blockwise attention eliminates.

blocks.md: Memory is only half the wall. The *GPU and inference basics* course counts about $2N$ FLOPs per token for the weights and $4\,n_{\text{layer}}\,n_{\text{ctx}}\,d_{\text{attn}}$ for attention (a dot product with each earlier key, then a weighted sum of values). For Llama 3 8B, $N \approx 7.5$B weights sit in matrix multiplies (32 layers of 218M plus the 128K-vocabulary output layer), so the weights cost 15.0 GFLOP per token, while attention costs $4 \times 32 \times n_{\text{ctx}} \times 4096 = 524{,}288\,n_{\text{ctx}}$. The two are equal at $n_{\text{ctx}} \approx 28{,}600$ tokens.

blocks.title: Llama 3 8B FLOPs per token: weights vs attention

scenes.caption: Below about 28,600 tokens of context the weights dominate each token's work. Above it, attention does.
At 128K a token's attention costs 68.7 GFLOP, 4.6 times its weight work; at 1M it is 550 GFLOP, 37 times. Context parallelism exists for this term as much as for memory.

blocks.md:
**Prefill**, processing the whole prompt before the first output token, sums that per-token cost over a causal triangle: about $2N n + 2\,n_{\text{layer}}\,d_{\text{attn}}\,n^2$ FLOPs for an $n$-token prompt. For Llama 3 8B that is 0.77 PFLOP at 32K (36% attention), 6.5 PFLOP at 128K (70%) and 304 PFLOP at 1M (95%; 1M is beyond this model's trained length, so it is only a cost estimate). At an assumed 500 TFLOP/s sustained on one H100, the time to first token would be 1.5 s, 12.9 s and about 10 minutes.

Measured, from Meta's *Context Parallelism for Scalable Million-Token Inference* (Yang et al., 2024): Llama 3 405B, with FP8 weights in its feed-forward layers, prefilled 1M tokens in 77 s and 128K in 3.8 s on 16 nodes of 8 H100s, at 93% parallelization efficiency. Their count, $4.9 \times 10^{18}$ FLOPs for 1M tokens with $4.1 \times 10^{18}$ of it attention, means 502 TFLOP/s per GPU. One GPU at that rate would need about 2.7 hours, which is why lesson 6 covers context parallelism for inference.

Blockwise attention works because softmax can be computed **incrementally**. A query's softmax weight on key $i$ is $e^{s_i}/\sum_j e^{s_j}$, where $s_i$ is its score with key $i$. Exponentials of large scores overflow, so implementations subtract the largest score $m$ first; the factor $e^{-m}$ appears on top and bottom and cancels, so the weights do not change. Here $m$ is a running maximum, not a position as in lessons 1 to 4. The optional *FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4* course (outside this course's prerequisites) derives this online softmax in full; here is the short version.

Keep three numbers per query: the running maximum score $m$, the running denominator $\ell = \sum e^{s_i - m}$ and the running unnormalized output $o = \sum e^{s_i - m} v_i$. When a new block arrives with a larger maximum, rescale the old $\ell$ and $o$ by $e^{m_{old} - m_{new}}$. This works because $e^{s_i - m_{old}} \cdot e^{m_{old} - m_{new}} = e^{s_i - m_{new}}$: every old term is re-expressed against the new maximum. The final answer is $o/\ell$, identical to the full softmax. Crucially, blocks can be merged in **any order**.

blocks.title: Merging two KV blocks with an online softmax
blocks.code:
import math
def merge(state, scores, values):
    m, l, o = state
    m_new = max(m, max(scores))
    c = math.exp(m - m_new)      # rescale old sums
    l = l * c + sum(math.exp(x - m_new) for x in scores)
    o = o * c + sum(math.exp(x - m_new) * v for x, v in zip(scores, values))
    return m_new, l, o

state = (-math.inf, 0.0, 0.0)
state = merge(state, [2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0])  # local KV block
state = merge(state, [3.0, 0.5], [3.0, 4.0])  # block from neighbor
m, l, o = state
print(round(o / l, 4))

scenes.caption: Start empty: m = minus infinity, l = 0, o = 0. One query will see 4 keys split into two blocks of 2.
Local block: scores 2.0 and 1.0, values 1 and 2. m = 2, l = 1 + e^-1 = 1.3679, o = 1 + 2e^-1 = 1.7358. Partial answer o / l = 1.2689.
Block from the neighbour: scores 3.0 and 0.5. New max 3, so old sums are rescaled by e^(2-3) = 0.3679 before adding. l = 1.5853, o = 3.9669.
o / l = 2.5023, exactly the output of a full softmax over all 4 scores (weights 0.232, 0.085, 0.631, 0.052). No 4-wide score row was ever stored.

blocks.md: **Ring Attention** (Liu, Zaharia, Abbeel, 2023) turns this order freedom into a distributed algorithm. Split the sequence into $N$ blocks and give host $i$ (one accelerator, a GPU or TPU chip) block $i$: its queries, keys and values. Arrange hosts in a ring. At each step every host computes blockwise attention of its *local queries* against the KV block it currently holds, and at the same time sends that KV block to the next host and receives one from the previous host. After $N$ steps every query block has met every KV block, and the result is **exact** attention.

blocks.title: Ring Attention with 4 hosts: KV blocks rotate, queries stay

scenes.caption: Step 1: host i attends its query block Qi to its own KV block KVi, while already sending KVi to host i+1 (dots on the arrows).
Step 2: each host now holds its predecessor's block. Host 0 attends Q0 to KV3, host 1 attends Q1 to KV0, and the next transfer is already in flight.

Step 3: blocks have travelled two hops. Only neighbour to neighbour links are used, so this maps onto GPU fabrics linking every GPU to every other and onto TPU torus links (a grid whose rows wrap around) alike.
Step 4: last block, no further send. Every host has merged all 4 KV blocks into its online softmax, then runs the feedforward on its own block. Then the next layer starts.

blocks.prompt: Each host must hold its query block, the KV block it is computing on, a buffer for the KV block arriving, and its output. With block size c, batch size b (not the RoPE base) and hidden size h in bf16, how does per-host activation memory depend on the total sequence length?
blocks.reveal: It does not. The paper counts six blocks of $b \times c \times h$ numbers: 1 for queries, 2 for current K and V, 2 for the incoming K and V, 1 for the output. It writes this as 6bch bytes per layer; in bf16, at 2 bytes per number, it is 12bch bytes. Either way it is a constant times $c$. Total sequence length only changes how many hosts (or steps) you need. That is why maximum context scales with device count: in their experiments 8 A100s gave 8x the previous best and TPUv4-1024 gave up to 512x.

blocks.md: **The backward pass.** Ring Attention is mostly used for training, so gradients must flow too. Each host keeps its query block and accumulates the query gradient $dQ_i$ locally. The KV blocks go around the ring a second time, and each host recomputes its attention on the block it holds (the forward did not store the scores) and adds that block's contribution to $dK_j$ and $dV_j$. Those two gradient accumulators travel *with* their K and V block, so after $N$ steps they arrive back at the host that owns block $j$, complete. The paper's JAX code permutes exactly four arrays per step: `k, v, dk, dv`.

blocks.title: Ring Attention backward: gradients ride with their KV block

scenes.caption: Step 1: host i recomputes attention of Qi against its own block, adds to dQi, and starts dKi and dVi. All four arrays leave for host i+1.
Step 2: host 0 now holds block 3 and its partial dK3, dV3. It adds Q0's contribution to them and to dQ0, then passes them on.
After N = 4 steps every block has met every query block and its gradient is back home: dKi, dVi on host i, plus dQi, which never moved.

blocks.md: Does the backward pass still hide its traffic? In the next lesson's symbols (block size $c$ tokens, hidden size $d$, per-host compute $F$ FLOP/s, link bandwidth $B$ bytes/s), a forward step does $4dc^2$ FLOPs and sends $4cd$ bytes of bf16 K and V, which stays hidden when $c \ge F/B$. Backward sends four arrays instead of two, and the paper's TPU (Pallas) kernel keeps $dK$ and $dV$ in FP32: $4cd$ bytes for K and V plus $8cd$ for the gradients, $12cd$ in all, three times the forward. But the backward also does more math: five block matrix multiplies (recompute the scores, then $dV$, $dP$ (the gradient of the softmax weights), $dQ$ and $dK$) instead of two, so $10dc^2$ FLOPs, 2.5 times the forward. The condition becomes $c \ge 1.2\,F/B$, only slightly stricter; with gradients kept in bf16, as in the paper's plain JAX version, it is $c \ge 0.8\,F/B$. The paper notes its overlap applies to both passes.

Ring Attention is not an approximation like sparse attention (each query sees only a chosen subset of keys) or sliding-window attention (each query sees only a fixed window of recent tokens). Each query still attends to every key; only the *order* and *location* of the work change. It also does not reduce FLOPs: total compute is the same quadratic amount, just spread over more chips.

Online softmax makes attention over KV blocks order-independent. Ring Attention exploits that: queries stay put, KV blocks travel around the ring, and each host needs memory proportional to its block, not to the full sequence.

blocks.question: With Ring Attention on N hosts, after how many compute steps has host 0's query block seen every KV block of the sequence (one layer, forward pass)?
options: N
log2 N
N squared
blocks.explain: Each step delivers one new KV block from the predecessor. Host 0 starts with its own block and needs N - 1 more hops, so N compute steps in total (Algorithm 1 loops over the N - 1 transfers).

blocks.question: A KV block arrives whose maximum score (5.0) exceeds the running maximum (3.0). What must the online softmax do with its existing denominator l and output o?
options: Multiply both by e^(3 - 5) before adding the new terms
Discard them and restart from the new block
Multiply only o by e^(5 - 3)
Nothing; maxima only matter for the final normalization
blocks.explain: Old terms were exponentiated relative to max 3. To express them relative to the new max 5, multiply by e^(3-5) = e^-2. Then add the new block's terms computed with max 5. Skipping this gives wrong weights.

blocks.question: A Llama 3 8B deployment wants to prefill 128K-token prompts. Roughly what share of the prefill FLOPs is attention rather than weight matrix multiplies?
options: About 5%: weights always dominate
Exactly 50%, by symmetry
About 70%
About 99%
blocks.explain: Weights: 2N x n = 15.0 GFLOP x 131,072 = 1.97 PFLOP. Attention: 2 x 32 x 4096 x 131,072 squared = 4.50 PFLOP. Attention is 4.50 / 6.47 = 70%. The share keeps rising with length: 36% at 32K, 95% at 1M.

lessons.title: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses

blocks.md: Ring Attention is only free if sending a KV block takes no longer than computing on it. The paper's arithmetic, for block size $c$ (tokens), hidden size $d$ (not the RoPE pair index from earlier lessons), per-host compute $F$ (FLOP/s) and link bandwidth $B$ (bytes/s): blockwise attention costs $2dc^2$ FLOPs for $QK^\top$ plus $2dc^2$ for multiplying by $V$, and the K and V blocks are $2cd$ bytes each in bf16. Where these come from: multiplying the $c \times d$ query block by the $d \times c$ transposed key block takes $c^2$ dot products of length $d$, each $d$ multiplies and $d$ adds, so $2dc^2$; multiplying the $c \times c$ weights by the $c \times d$ value block costs the same again. A K or V block holds $c \times d$ numbers at 2 bytes each.

blocks.caption: Ring Attention Sec. 3. Compute time 4dc squared over F must be at least the transfer time 4cd over B; dividing both sides by 4cd leaves c at least F over B. The hidden size cancels: the minimum block depends only on the hardware's FLOPs-to-bandwidth ratio.

blocks.md: Plug in an A100 (312 TFLOP/s bf16 peak, as in the paper's Table 2): over NVLink, NVIDIA's direct GPU-to-GPU link inside one server, at 300 GB/s, $c \ge 312\times10^{12}/300\times10^{9} = 1{,}040$ tokens; over InfiniBand, a network between servers, at 12.5 GB/s, $c \ge 24{,}960$. The paper then asks for a per-host sequence of about $6c$ (6,240 and 149,760 tokens; the paper's Table 2 prints 6.2K and 149.5K). Worked example with $c = 4096$, $d = 4096$: compute takes $4 \cdot 4096^3 / 312\times10^{12} = 0.881$ ms, the K plus V block of $4cd$ = 67.1 MB takes 0.224 ms on NVLink but 5.37 ms on InfiniBand.

blocks.title: One host in a 4-host ring, c = 4096, d = 4096 (simplified)

scenes.caption: NVLink: each 0.224 ms transfer hides under a 0.881 ms compute step. Four steps finish at 3.52 ms, exactly the pure compute time.
InfiniBand at 12.5 GB/s: each transfer takes 5.37 ms, so compute idles waiting for the next block. The same work ends at about 17 ms, almost 5x slower. Here c = 4096 is far below F/B = 24,960.

blocks.md: **With grouped-query attention** the transfer shrinks but the compute does not. K and V have only $H_{kv} d_{\text{head}}$ columns instead of $d$, so the condition becomes $c \ge (H_{kv}/H)\,F/B$. Llama 3 8B has $H = 32$ query heads and $H_{kv} = 8$ KV heads of 128, so K and V are 1,024 wide against a 4,096 hidden size: on the A100 the minimum block drops to 260 tokens over NVLink and 6,240 over InfiniBand (the same number as the 6c sequence above only by coincidence). In the worked example the K plus V block falls from 67.1 MB to 16.8 MB, 1.34 ms over InfiniBand instead of 5.37 ms. The optional *Megatron-Core* course (outside this course's prerequisites) derives the same rule for its balanced causal split as $c \ge 2(H_{kv}/H)(F/B)$; the 2 appears because an off-diagonal step there computes only half a block.

blocks.title: Compute versus transfer time per ring step

scenes.caption: A100 over NVLink: transfer grows linearly in c, compute quadratically. They cross at c = F/B = 1,040 tokens; beyond it the transfer is hidden.
Drop bandwidth to 12.5 GB/s (InfiniBand in the paper's table): the crossover moves to 24,960 tokens, so each host needs much longer blocks to stay compute bound.

blocks.md: **Causal masking breaks the balance.** In a decoder, query block $i$ only needs KV blocks $0..i$. With contiguous blocks, host 0 has almost nothing to do while the last host does a full row of work, yet the ring advances in lockstep. **Striped Attention** (Brandon et al., 2023) fixes this by giving each device tokens spread uniformly through the sequence, reporting up to 1.45x end-to-end speedup at 256K on A100s and TPUv4s. Llama 3 uses a related trick. Its **context parallelism** (CP) splits one long sequence across a group of GPUs, each holding a slice of the tokens through every layer (Ring Attention is one way to do this); CP also names the group's size, and each GPU's index in the group is its rank. Split the sequence into $2 \times CP$ chunks and give rank $i$ chunks $i$ and $2 \times CP - 1 - i$. The *Megatron-Core* course shows how its context parallelism implements this split (`get_batch_on_this_cp_rank`).

blocks.title: Causal attention work by rank (8 chunks, 4 ranks): value = owning rank

scenes.caption: Contiguous split: rank 0 owns query chunks 0 and 1, rank 3 owns 6 and 7. Masked (upper) cells are skipped. Rank 3's rows are the longest.
Llama 3 style zigzag: rank i owns chunks i and 7 - i. Each rank now gets one short row and one long row.

blocks.title: Causal work per rank, in chunk-pairs (diagonal counts as half)

scenes.caption: Contiguous: 2, 6, 10, 14. The step time is set by the busiest rank, so ranks 0 to 2 idle most of the time.
Zigzag (chunks i and 7 - i): 8, 8, 8, 8. Same total of 32, perfectly balanced.

blocks.md: Llama 3 also did **not** use a ring: its context parallelism first **all-gathers** K and V (a collective step in which every rank sends its piece to all the others, so every rank ends with the full K and V), then computes attention for the local query chunk. The paper accepts the exposed communication (transfer time not hidden behind compute) because all-gather makes masks such as document masks easy (masks that stop tokens attending across the boundary between documents packed into one sequence), and with grouped-query attention K and V are much smaller than Q, while for sequence length $S$ attention compute is $O(S^2)$ against $O(S)$ for the gather.

**DeepSpeed Ulysses** (Jacobs et al., 2023), part of Microsoft's DeepSpeed training library, takes a different route. Each GPU holds a sequence shard; before attention an **all-to-all** (a collective step in which every GPU sends a different piece to every other GPU) reshuffles Q, K and V so each GPU holds the *full sequence* for a subset of heads, runs ordinary attention, and a second all-to-all returns to sequence sharding. For hidden size $h$, Q, K and V are each $N \times h$, so the step moves $3Nh$ in, plus $Nh$ for the output, and an all-to-all of a message $M$ over $P$ GPUs moves $M/P$ per link. Per-link volume is $4Nh/P$, constant when sequence length $N$ and GPUs $P$ grow together.

blocks.title: Ulysses all-to-all on 4 GPUs (T = token chunk, H = head)

scenes.caption: Before attention: GPU g holds token chunk g for all 4 heads (sequence parallel layout).
After the all-to-all: GPU g holds head g for all 4 token chunks, so it can run exact attention for that head locally. A second all-to-all reverses this after attention.

blocks.md: Choosing a scheme: Ulysses splits by heads, so (following from its layout) its parallel degree cannot exceed the number of heads, and every GPU still holds the full sequence for its heads. Ring Attention has no head limit and keeps per-device memory proportional to the block, but needs blocks above F/B and load balancing for causal masks. All-gather CP (Llama 3) is simplest and handles arbitrary masks, at the cost of exposed communication.

**Context parallelism for inference.** Serving a long prompt has the same two walls, and Meta's inference paper (Yang et al., 2024) applies ring attention to prefill and decode with load-balanced sharding. One choice matters that training never faces: *which* tensor travels. **Pass-KV** keeps queries still and rotates K and V, as above. **Pass-Q** keeps each rank's slice of the KV cache still and rotates the queries; partial outputs then end up scattered, so an all-to-all sends them, with their log-sum-exp $m + \ln \ell$ (the running max and denominator in one number), back to the query's owner, where the online-softmax rule from lesson 5 merges them. Send the smaller tensor: with $T$ new tokens and $P$ cached ones, pass-KV moves less data when $T/(T+P) \ge 2H_{kv}/H$. That threshold is 0.5 for Llama 3 8B and 0.125 for Llama 3 405B (128 query heads, 8 KV heads).

blocks.title: 200-token follow-up on a cached 500K context, one layer (simplified)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: Llama 3 405B shapes, CP = 4 ranks, 50 GB/s per rank (400 Gb/s RDMA), 500 TFLOP/s, no tensor parallelism. Pass-KV: each step ships 512 MB of cached K and V (10.24 ms) for 0.82 ms of attention, so compute waits.
Pass-Q: each step ships the 50 visiting queries, 1.64 MB (0.03 ms), hidden under the same 0.82 ms of attention. Four steps plus a small all-to-all of partial outputs: about 3.3 ms instead of 31.5.

blocks.md: Decode is the extreme case: $T = 1$ new token per sequence, so passing Q is almost always smaller, and Meta uses pass-Q for decode and for partial prefill with a high cache hit rate, pass-KV for full prefill. Each rank attends over its own shard of the KV cache and the partial results are merged with the same log-sum-exp rule. The paper measured the switch point on 128K contexts at about 5% new tokens (6,400 of 128K). The trade is not free: at 128K, CP over 2 and 4 nodes cut time to first token from 42.0 s to 21.0 s and 11.0 s, but time per output token rose from 46 ms to 60 ms and 71 ms. Shrinking that cache is the subject of the optional *KV cache compression and quantization* course.

Overlap condition: $c \ge F/B$. Fast links (NVLink, the TPU inter-chip interconnect or ICI) need blocks of about 1K tokens; slow links need tens of thousands. Causal masks require striping or zigzag chunk assignment, or the busiest rank sets the pace.

blocks.question: You move a Ring Attention job from NVLink (300 GB/s) to a 25 GB/s network with the same GPUs (312 TFLOP/s). Roughly what minimum block size now hides communication?
options: 1,040 tokens, unchanged since hidden size cancels
About 87 tokens
About 12,480 tokens
It can never be hidden on a slower link
blocks.explain: c >= F / B = 312e12 / 25e9 = 12,480. Bandwidth dropped 12x, so the minimum block grows 12x. The hidden size cancels, but the bandwidth does not.

blocks.question: Ring Attention with 4 ranks and contiguous chunks shows rank 3 at full utilization and rank 0 mostly idle on a causal model. Which change fixes this without changing the math?
options: Increase the block size c
Assign each rank tokens or chunks spread across the sequence (striped or zigzag)
Switch to bidirectional attention
Reduce the number of KV heads
blocks.explain: The imbalance comes from the causal triangle: later query chunks attend to more keys. Striped Attention or Llama 3's chunk i plus chunk 2CP - 1 - i assignment gives every rank the same amount of unmasked work.

blocks.question: Why does DeepSpeed Ulysses' per-link communication stay constant as you scale sequence length and GPU count together?
options: It compresses activations to 1 bit
It only communicates the KV cache once per training run
It never communicates; each GPU attends locally
An all-to-all over P GPUs moves M/P per link, and the message M = 4Nh grows with N at the same rate as P
blocks.explain: Per-link volume is 4Nh/P. Doubling both N and P leaves it unchanged. With h = 4096 and N = 32K tokens per GPU, that is about 1.07 GB per layer in bf16 at P = 2, 4, 8 or 16.

blocks.question: A user asks a 200-token follow-up question about a 500K-token document whose KV cache is already sharded across 4 context-parallel ranks (Llama 3 405B). Which tensor should circulate in the ring?
options: K and V, as in training, since Ring Attention always passes KV
Neither: gather the entire cache onto one GPU first
Both Q and KV, alternating steps
Q, because the 200 new tokens' queries are far smaller than the cached K and V
blocks.explain: New-token share T/(T+P) = 200/500,200 = 0.0004, far below the 2 x 8/128 = 0.125 threshold. Each pass-KV step would ship about 512 MB of cache per rank, pass-Q about 1.6 MB of queries, plus one all-to-all to return the partial outputs for merging.

lessons.title: Build it: YaRN tables and a four-host ring in NumPy

blocks.md: Two small programs make lessons 2, 3, 5 and 6 concrete, and both run on a laptop CPU in about a second with only NumPy. The first computes the RoPE frequency tables for Llama 2 under PI, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN, the way the Hugging Face transformers code does. The second simulates Ring Attention on four pretend hosts and checks it against plain causal attention, first with contiguous blocks and then with the zigzag split. Everything here is real output from running the code.

blocks.code:
import math, numpy as np
D, b, L, s, alpha, beta = 128, 10000.0, 4096, 16, 1, 32
d = np.arange(D // 2)
theta = b ** (-2 * d / D)                  # original inv_freq
r = L / (2 * math.pi / theta)              # turns during training
pi = theta / s                             # Position Interpolation
ntk = (b * s ** (D / (D - 2))) ** (-2 * d / D)   # NTK-aware base change
g = np.clip((r - alpha) / (beta - alpha), 0, 1)  # paper: ramp in r
yarn = (1 - g) * theta / s + g * theta
# Hugging Face: ramp in pair index between floor/ceil of the r-boundaries
def corr_dim(rot): return D * math.log(L / (rot * 2 * math.pi)) / (2 * math.log(b))
lo, hi = math.floor(corr_dim(beta)), math.ceil(corr_dim(alpha))
ramp = np.clip((d - lo) / (hi - lo), 0, 1)
hf = ramp * theta / s + (1 - ramp) * theta
mscale = 0.1 * math.log(s) + 1
print("HF ramp pairs", lo, "to", hi, " attention factor", round(mscale, 4))
for i in (0, 16, 20, 32, 40, 46, 63):   # pair, then multiplier: PI NTK YaRN HF
    print(i, *(round(x / theta[i], 4) for x in (pi[i], ntk[i], yarn[i], hf[i])))
blocks.caption: Llama 2 (|D| = 128, base 10,000, L = 4,096) extended with s = 16. Prints each method's frequency multiplier theta' / theta for a few pairs.
Output. Columns: pair, PI, NTK-aware, YaRN as in the paper (ramp in r), YaRN as in Hugging Face (ramp in pair index).

blocks.md:
Read it row by row. PI divides every pair by 16 (0.0625). NTK-aware slows pair 16 about 2x and pair 32 about 4x. The paper's YaRN keeps pairs 0 to 20 and fully interpolates from pair 46, as lesson 3 said. The last two columns agree at the ends and disagree in the middle: pair 32 keeps 0.2294 of its frequency in the paper's rule and 0.5673 in Hugging Face's. Hugging Face finds where $r$ crosses 32 and 1 (pairs 20.94 and 45.03), rounds out to 20 and 46, and ramps linearly in *pair index* between them; the paper ramps linearly in $r$, which is exponential in the pair index.

To check against the library itself, build a `LlamaConfig` with `rope_parameters={"rope_type": "yarn", "rope_theta": 10000.0, "factor": 16.0, "original_max_position_embeddings": 4096}` and call `ROPE_INIT_FUNCTIONS["yarn"](cfg, "cpu")` from `transformers.modeling_rope_utils`. We ran it (transformers 5.24 on CPU): it returned attention factor 1.2773 and multipliers 0.5673 at pair 32 and 0.2788 at pair 40, matching the last column. The `llama3` entry returned 29 kept, 6 smoothed and 29 divided pairs, as in lesson 3.

The paper's YaRN and Hugging Face's YaRN are different functions in the middle pairs. A checkpoint fine-tuned under one and served under the other sees frequencies it was not trained with. When porting a model between frameworks, compare the generated inv_freq tables, not just the config keys.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, c, d = 4, 64, 16                      # hosts, block size, head dim
S = N * c
q, k, v = (rng.standard_normal((S, d)) for _ in range(3))

def reference(q, k, v):                  # full causal attention
    s = q @ k.T / np.sqrt(d)
    s[np.triu_indices(S, 1)] = -np.inf
    p = np.exp(s - s.max(1, keepdims=True))
    return (p / p.sum(1, keepdims=True)) @ v

def merge(m, l, o, s, vb):               # online softmax, one KV block
    m_new = np.maximum(m, s.max(1))
    c_old, p = np.exp(m - m_new), np.exp(s - m_new[:, None])
    return m_new, l * c_old + p.sum(1), o * c_old[:, None] + p @ vb

def ring(q, k, v):
    Q = [q[i*c:(i+1)*c] for i in range(N)]      # queries never move
    KV = [(k[i*c:(i+1)*c], v[i*c:(i+1)*c], i) for i in range(N)]
    st = [(np.full(c, -np.inf), np.zeros(c), np.zeros((c, d))) for _ in range(N)]
    for step in range(N):
        for i in range(N):
            kb, vb, j = KV[i]                   # host i holds block j
            if j > i: continue                  # future block: skip
            s = Q[i] @ kb.T / np.sqrt(d)
            if j == i:                          # diagonal: causal mask
                s[np.triu_indices(c, 1)] = -np.inf
            st[i] = merge(*st[i], s, vb)
        KV = [KV[(i - 1) % N] for i in range(N)]  # pass KV to next host
    return np.concatenate([o / l[:, None] for m, l, o in st])

out = ring(q, k, v)
print("max |ring - full| =", np.abs(out - reference(q, k, v)).max())

scenes.caption: Each host keeps its 64 queries and starts with its own K, V block, tagged with its block number j. State per host: running max, denominator and output.
Step 0, host 0 holds block 0: the diagonal block. Mask the upper triangle (query t sees keys up to t), then merge. All 64 rows of host 0 are now final.
After the step every block moves one host forward: host 0 receives block 3 from host 3.
Steps 1 to 3, host 0 holds blocks 3, 2, then 1. Each is a future block (j > i), so host 0 skips it and sits idle while host 3 does real work every step.
Finally each host divides o by l. Concatenated, the blocks match full causal attention to 5e-16: floating-point rounding, nothing more.

blocks.prompt: Count the block-pairs each host computes over the four steps of the contiguous ring above (a diagonal block counts as half). What do you get for hosts 0 to 3?
blocks.reveal: 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5. Host i computes its diagonal block plus i earlier blocks; host 3 does seven times host 0's work, and the lockstep ring waits for host 3. The next program splits the sequence into 8 chunks and gives host i chunks i and 7 - i, the zigzag assignment from lesson 6.

blocks.code:
from ring_sim import np, N, S, d, q, k, v, merge, reference
C = 2 * N; w = S // C                          # 8 chunks of 32 tokens
own = {"contiguous": [[2*i, 2*i + 1] for i in range(N)],
       "zigzag": [[i, C - 1 - i] for i in range(N)]}   # chunks i and 2CP-1-i

for name, chunks in own.items():
    pos = [np.concatenate([np.arange(a*w, (a+1)*w) for a in ch]) for ch in chunks]
    st = [(np.full(len(p), -np.inf), np.zeros(len(p)), np.zeros((len(p), d))) for p in pos]
    work = [0.0] * N
    for step in range(N):
        for i in range(N):
            j = (i - step) % N                  # whose KV host i holds now
            s = q[pos[i]] @ k[pos[j]].T / np.sqrt(d)
            s[pos[i][:, None] < pos[j][None, :]] = -np.inf   # causal by position
            work[i] += (s > -np.inf).sum() / (w * w)
            st[i] = merge(*st[i], s, v[pos[j]])
    out = np.zeros((S, d))
    for i in range(N):
        m, l, o = st[i]; out[pos[i]] = o / l[:, None]
    err = np.abs(out - reference(q, k, v)).max()
    print(name, "work per host:", [round(float(x), 1) for x in work], "err %.1e" % err)

blocks.question: A teammate's ring simulation matches full attention when the mask is off, but with a causal mask 252 of 256 rows are wrong; only the last row of each 64-token block is right. Which block-level rule did they most likely forget?
options: Skipping future blocks (j > i)
Rescaling l and o when the running max grows
Masking the upper triangle inside the diagonal block (j = i)
Passing KV to host i + 1 instead of i - 1
blocks.explain: We ran exactly this bug: without the diagonal mask every query sees the later keys of its own block, except the block's last token, which legitimately sees all 64. Forgetting the j > i skip instead corrupts whole blocks (error 1.9 in our run). A wrong rescale would break the unmasked case too.

blocks.md: Both halves of the course fit in about 60 lines: the frequency table is a per-pair multiplier on inv_freq (check it against the library you serve with), and Ring Attention is an online-softmax merge over blocks in any order, with one masking rule per block: past blocks in full, the diagonal block causally, future blocks skipped.

lessons.title: Does the model use its context? Evaluation

blocks.md: A model that *accepts* 128K tokens is not necessarily a model that *uses* them. Perplexity, the usual long-context metric in extension papers (YaRN reports sliding-window perplexity, which scores a long document in overlapping windows so every token is predicted with a long stretch of preceding text, on Proof-pile and on GovReport, a dataset of long US government reports), mostly rewards predicting the next token from nearby text. It can keep improving while retrieval from far away silently fails. So long-context work is evaluated with tasks where the answer can only come from a specific distant spot.

- **Passkey retrieval** (used by PI and YaRN): hide a five-digit number in filler text and ask for it. YaRN reports its 128K Llama 2 model passes with very high accuracy across the whole window.
- **Needle in a haystack**: the same idea with a sentence planted at varying depths and lengths. Llama 3 reports 100% retrieval at all depths and lengths, and also a multi-needle variant (4 needles, retrieve 2).
- **Position-controlled question answering**: Lost in the Middle (Liu et al., 2023) moves the document containing the answer through 10, 20 or 30 retrieved documents. This is the setup of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where a search step pastes documents relevant to the question into the prompt.

blocks.title: GPT-3.5-Turbo accuracy by answer position, 20 docs

scenes.caption: Answer document first: 75.8%. Answer last: 63.2%. This is the U-shape: primacy (the start) and recency (the end) are strong (Lost in the Middle, Table 6).
Answer in the middle (position 10): 53.8%, below the 56.1% the model scores with no documents at all (closed-book). Adding the right document in the wrong place made it worse than adding nothing.

blocks.prompt: The 16K-context version of GPT-3.5-Turbo was also tested on the same 20-document prompts (about 3K tokens on average, which fit in both). Would you expect the 16K model to use the middle documents better?
blocks.reveal: No. The paper finds the extended-context model's curve nearly superimposed on the standard one (for example 54.1% vs 53.8% at position 10). A bigger window raises the ceiling on what fits, not how well the model uses what is inside it.

blocks.md: **RULER** (Hsieh et al., 2024) generalizes needle tests into 13 synthetic tasks in four categories: retrieval (with multiple keys, values and distractors), multi-hop tracing (follow a chain of variable assignments to find every name bound to a value), aggregation (find the most frequent words in a long list), and question answering, at configurable lengths. It defines a model's **effective length** as the longest tested length whose average score stays above Llama 2 7B's score at 4K, 85.6%. Of 17 models claiming 32K or more, only about half held that threshold at 32K.

blocks.title: RULER average score by length (Table 3); threshold 85.6%

scenes.caption: Llama 3.1 8B, claimed 128K: drops below 85.6% after 32K (84.7% at 64K), so its effective length is 32K.
Mistral 7B v0.2, claimed 32K: 75.4% at 32K and 13.8% at 128K, effective length 16K. Both score near-perfectly on passkey and vanilla needle tests at their claimed lengths.
Gemini 1.5 Pro, claimed 1M: 94.4% even at 128K, effective length above 128K, the longest length tested. Some models do hold up; you have to measure.

blocks.md: Putting the pieces together, the Llama 3 report shows what a production recipe checks. Llama 3 405B grew its context in **six stages** from 8K to 128K using about **800B tokens** of long-context pretraining, and moved to the next stage only when (1) short-context evaluations had fully recovered and (2) the model perfectly solved needle-in-a-haystack up to the current length. It also masks attention between different documents packed into one sequence, which it found important for continued pretraining on very long sequences. Lesson 4 covers the base-frequency and data choices behind such stages.

Do not trust a single number. Low perplexity, a passing passkey test and a large advertised window can all coexist with poor use of mid-context information. Test retrieval at many depths, multi-hop and aggregation tasks, and short-context regressions.

Extending RoPE (PI, NTK, YaRN) makes long positions *in distribution*; Ring Attention and context parallelism make long sequences *fit*; neither guarantees the model *uses* the context. Measure effective length with depth-controlled tasks such as RULER.

blocks.question: A team extends a 4K model to 64K with YaRN. Perplexity on long documents improves steadily up to 64K, and a single-needle test passes at every depth. What is the most informative next evaluation?
options: Run harder tasks (multi-key retrieval, multi-hop tracing, aggregation) across lengths, plus short-context benchmarks for regressions
Nothing, both checks passed
Report perplexity at 128K too
Retrain from scratch at 64K to be sure
blocks.explain: RULER shows models that pass vanilla needle tests still drop sharply on harder tasks as length grows. Llama 3 also gated each stage on recovering short-context quality. Perplexity rewards local prediction and says little about distant retrieval.

blocks.question: In Lost in the Middle (20 documents, GPT-3.5-Turbo), where should a RAG system place the most relevant retrieved passage?
options: In the middle, so the model reads context on both sides
At the very beginning (or end) of the context
It does not matter for models with a 16K window
Randomly, to avoid bias
blocks.explain: Accuracy was 75.8% with the answer first and 63.2% last, but 53.8% in the middle, below closed-book. The bigger 16K variant showed the same curve.
